item.title: China to accelerate deep-sea development during 15th Five-Year Plan period as marine economy projected to reach 13 trillion yuan by 2030
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 17:51:00
China's upgraded manned deep-sea submersible Jiaolong is recovered on October 2, 2026, after completing its 465th dive, during which it reached a depth of 7,056.9 meters. Photo: Xinhua China will continue to accelerate deep-sea mineral development, natural gas hydrate extraction, and ultra-deep marine oil and gas exploration during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) said on Tuesday. The country will implement major projects, including the third phases of the manned deep-sea submersible Jiaolong and icebreakers Xuelong's polar expedition programs. These initiatives aim to drive technological breakthroughs, equipment upgrades and commercialization across the marine sector. Ma Weichen, a NDRC official, said at a press conference that the 15th Five-Year Plan period is a critical window for China to become a maritime power. The country will focus on three areas - new technology, new industries and new frontiers. On technology, China will organize research on key marine challenges, develop more equipment, and address gaps in high-end instruments, critical materials and basic software. The country will also coordinate the development of national laboratories, key laboratories and engineering projects, while training more talent. In the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, China's marine GDP surpassed 9 trillion yuan, 10 trillion yuan and 11 trillion yuan in successive steps. The China Marine Economic Development Report 2026 shows that marine GDP exceeded 11 trillion yuan in 2025, accounting for 7.9 percent of national GDP. China leads the world in shipbuilding, marine engineering equipment and ocean shipping. Major achievements include the commissioning of the world's largest ocean drilling vessel Mengxiang, and the first crewed submersible mission in the Arctic ice zone. In the next phase, China will consolidate marine equipment manufacturing, transportation and fisheries, while fostering new sectors such as marine biomedicine, new marine materials, marine electronics and artificial intelligence applications, the official said. Offshore wind power will expand in an orderly manner, with integrated grid infrastructure. Cumulative installed offshore wind capacity is expected to exceed 100 million kilowatts by 2030. Marine GDP is projected to surpass 13 trillion yuan by 2030.

item.title: Police reprimand two women kimonos, samurai sword pose at Hunan Martyrs' Park
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 17:01:00
Photo: Screenshot from Sina Weibo A video showing two young women in kimonos with a prop samurai sword at Hunan Martyrs’ Park in Changsha, Central China’s Hunan Province, before being confronted by a passerby has drawn public attention. Local police later reprimanded the women, China Newsweek reported on Tuesday. In the video, one of the two young women, dressed as Tanjiro from Japanese anime series Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba, poses for photos on a park bridge with a prop samurai sword. A man confronts the pair, criticizing their costumes and props as inappropriate for the site. The two young women did not respond, covering their faces with umbrellas and ending the photo shoot before the video cut off. A park management office staff member told China Newsweek on Tuesday that both the sword and costumes were anime props. Park staff intervened after a complaint and asked them to leave, and local police later reprimanded them. Established in 1951 and opened in 1953, the Hunan Martyrs’ Park houses a memorial tower honoring 157 Hunan-born martyrs and a memorial hall displaying the stories and belongings of 90 revolutionary martyrs, including Yang Kaihui, Xia Minghan and Guo Liang. The site also preserves the names of more than 76,000 martyrs from across the province and is designated by the State Council as a major national martyrs' memorial site, Beijing Daily reported on Tuesday. The two women’s actions have drawn widespread online criticism, with many calling them disrespectful and describing the incident as a desecration of an important memorial site. The staff member said park authorities would normally step in when visitors show up in “unusual costumes,” but monitoring is difficult in an open park – especially when visitors change into such outfits after entering, Hongxing News reported. item.title: China's top economic planner pledges to take 'extraordinary measures' to drive new breakthroughs in key fields
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 16:49:00
A technician conducts chip quality inspections in a factory in Yiwu, East China's Zhejiang Province, in March 2026. Photo: VCG China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the top economic planner, said on Tuesday that it will accelerate its support for emerging pillar industries to promote high-quality economic development, pledging to take "extraordinary measures" to drive breakthroughs in key fields. The output value of the emerging pillar industries is projected to exceed 10 trillion yuan ($1.4 trillion) by the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), up from nearly 6 trillion yuan last year, Ren Zhongbao, an official with the NDRC, said at a press conference on Tuesday. Ren said the country will increase fiscal and financial support, and guide private capital into investing in emerging pillar industries. Meanwhile, China will support enterprises in taking the lead in implementing national science and technology projects and in building innovation platforms. China has identified six emerging pillar industries including integrated circuits, aerospace, and biomedicine to foster new growth levers during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. China will focus on quantum technology, bio-manufacturing, hydrogen energy, nuclear fusion energy, brain-computer interfaces, embodied intelligence and 6G telecommunications. It will also encourage regions to develop sub-sectors where they have comparative advantages, the NDRC said. Extraordinary measures will be taken to drive decisive breakthroughs in key areas across the entire industrial chain. Meanwhile, efforts will be made to promote the application of independently developed products and technologies, and foster a virtuous cycle in which real-world application drives further research and development, which in turn enables iterative tech upgrading, according to the NDRC. The initiative aims to break away from traditional research models, strengthen the role of enterprises as the main body of innovation, and improve funding allocation and support mechanisms for research teams, in a bid to counter external restrictions and achieve a high level of self-reliance in science and technology, Cao Heping, a professor at Peking University, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Cao said that amid intensifying global tech competition, China needs to further strengthen its capabilities in original innovation and basic research to address weaknesses in some technological fields. Wan Zhe, a professor at Beijing Normal University, told the Global Times on Tuesday that "extraordinary" does not simply mean piling on more resources or continuously scaling up input. Wan said it means reshaping research mechanisms by changing how work is organized, resources are allocated, talent is developed, and performance is evaluated. "When it comes to implementation, we need to start with the real pain points along the industrial chain. Technological, economic and security assessments should tell us which areas are genuinely strategic, and resources should flow precisely to the most critical links. We need to put enterprises genuinely in the driver's seat. That, in turn, calls for collaboration that cuts across sectors and disciplines," Wan said. "China's drive for technological breakthroughs has entered a critical new stage - moving from playing catch-up to running neck and neck with, and in some areas leading, global frontrunners. In other words, there is no longer a ready-made path to follow; we must rely on our own original exploration. That is why we need extraordinary patience from investors, an extraordinary model of organization, and an extraordinary tolerance for risk," Wan said. China's emerging pillar industries have maintained strong growth momentum, with research and development investment surging, new technologies and new products continuously emerging, and industrial scale expanding at an accelerating pace. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's integrated circuit output reached 442.8 billion units, up 23.3 percent year-on-year. The value of China's innovative drug out-licensing deals totaled $130 billion in the period, close to the total for all of last year, according to NDRC data.

item.title: 'Protectionism in disguise': Chinese experts blast US push to ban Chinese vehicles
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 16:46:00
Robots assemble a new-energy vehicle at Liuzhou Wuling Automobile Industry Co in Liuzhou, South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on July 18, 2026. Photo: VCG Chinese experts on Tuesday slammed a reported auto industry push for US lawmakers to pass a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles as "protectionism wrapped in the guise of national security." They warned that if the US keeps shutting itself off, it could ultimately fall behind in the global wave of vehicle electrification and intelligentization, to the detriment of consumers. According to Reuters, a group representing nearly all major automakers on Monday urged US lawmakers to pass a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles. In September, the Senate sponsors of the bipartisan effort to ban Chinese vehicles agreed to delay an effort to fast-track the bill until November despite overwhelming support. John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major automakers, claimed that "we need to protect the US market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in American communities." Washington's campaign against Chinese vehicles did not start with this bill. Back in 2025, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun already rejected the US restrictions on Chinese connected-vehicle software, hardware and complete vehicles on so-called national security grounds as "without any factual basis," and called the move typical protectionism and economic coercion. "The Alliance's push is essentially about blocking low-priced, high-value competitors from entering the market — economic protectionism, not a national security concern," He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Moreover, it claimed that Chinese vehicles pose "surveillance risk," but the allegation has never been backed by any publicly available evidence, He Weiwen said. Bozzella also cited major Chinese gains in the European market. According to him, in the first eight months of 2026, the EU imported more than 1.1 million vehicles from China — more than all of 2025. "Given the obvious national security risk and China's pattern of unfair behavior, Congress should protect our defense and advanced manufacturing base and stop Chinese automakers from doing here what they've gotten away with in Europe," Bozzella claimed. He Weiwen noted that Bozzella frames ordinary cost and technology competition as "national security" and "unfair practices," turning a blind eye to the US auto industry's own problems and invoking Europe's "market share shifts" to justify an even more extreme form of protectionism. US' own predicament Chinese experts say the US auto industry is grappling with multiple challenges, including a structural decline in competitiveness, policy uncertainty, high costs, and lagging behind in the global transition. US Federal Reserve data showed that in September this year, the capacity utilization rate for US automobile and light-duty motor vehicle manufacturing stood at just about 61.2 percent, down from 64.6 percent in August and remaining persistently low — evidence that the problem does not stem from "external shocks" but lies in a demand-supply mismatch rooted in weak product competitiveness, He Weiwen said. A combination of higher labor and battery costs, and tariffs along with rising chip and energy prices, is further pushing up costs, Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Moreover, sharp policy swings have left companies facing considerable uncertainty, Zhou said. According to Reuters, an array of automotive, environmental, trade and immigration policies of the Trump administration has undermined factory projects and employment in Lordstown and across America's heartland. Cancellations of EV projects and related battery facilities have snowballed, killing or jeopardizing tens of thousands of jobs, according to data from Atlas Public Policy, a research firm that tracks clean-energy investments. Acting in the name of an "innovation alliance" while pursuing a closed and conservative agenda will not protect the US auto industry — it will only blunt automakers' incentive to compete and innovate, Zhou warned. Moreover, the policy ban the Alliance is pushing runs sharply counter to real market demand. According to Reuters, related obstacles haven't quieted the buzz. The Cox survey polled 802 US consumers who expect to buy a car in the next two years. Nearly half - 49 percent - rated Chinese cars as having very good or excellent value, and 40 percent say they support the idea of Chinese auto brands in the US market. Rich Benoit, a car enthusiast whose YouTube videos reviewing Chinese models garner millions of views, said the most compelling feature is the price. He's considering buying a BYD model in Mexico and driving it across the border. "That's the only way to get one," Benoit said in the report. "They've been selling in Mexico for years... I want to own a Chinese EV in America." "Chinese EVs and smart vehicles hold clear advantages in price, range and intelligence. Can ignoring market demand and closing itself off really promote the healthy development of the industry?" Zhou asked, adding that a permanent ban would mean US consumers keep paying higher prices with fewer choices. What truly drives the auto industry forward is a stable market outlook, stronger incentives for companies to innovate and cooperate, and a commitment to openness and a level playing field, Zhou said. Electrification, connectivity and intelligentization have become the defining trends of the auto industry. The US auto industry now lags behind in the new energy space; by working with Chinese suppliers and drawing on China's industrial chain can it raise its own level, Zhang Xiang, a visiting professor in the engineering department of Zhengzhou-based Huanghe Science and Technology University, told the Global Times on Tuesday.

item.title: Yellow River, China's mother river, runs clearer after decades of conservation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 13:32:00
An aerial drone photo taken in Jixian County, north China's Shanxi Province, on Oct. 28, 2026, shows a rainbow over the Yellow River's Hukou Waterfall. (Photo by Lyu Guiming/Xinhua) The Hukou Waterfall on the Yellow River, once depicted on China's fourth-series 50-yuan banknotes as a torrent of muddy, turbulent water, now presents a markedly different scene, with its cascading waters running clear. Photographer Lyu Guiming, known for documenting the waterfall in Jixian County, Shanxi Province, since 1999, has witnessed the change. "Over the past decade, clear cascades at the waterfall have been my main photographic subject," Lyu said. "The contrast with the old scenes is striking." The changing waterscape reflects decades of efforts to protect and manage the Yellow River, China's second-longest river, which flows 5,464 km from its source in the highlands of Qinghai Province through nine provinces and autonomous regions, crossing deserts and loess lands before emptying into the Bohai Sea in Shandong Province, east China. In 1946, under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, an agency for people's Yellow River management was established on the river's banks in Heze, Shandong Province. Because Henan Province was frequently affected by flooding on the river, the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (YRCC) later moved its headquarters to Zhengzhou in December 1953. Thanks to 80 years of conservation efforts, the river, once prone to devastating floods, heavy sedimentation and shifting channels, now has cleaner waters and more sustainable water use. Historical records show that before the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the river's lower reaches experienced more than 1,500 dyke breaches and overflows and changed course 26 times. Sediment was a persistent challenge, giving rise to the old saying that half of a bowl of Yellow River water is sand. Wei Xiangyang, the commission's chief engineer, outlined progress in flood control, a central part of river management. Dykes built to withstand major floods now stretch 1,371 km in total along the lower reaches. Forty flood-control reservoirs on the river and its tributaries have a combined flood-control capacity of 19 billion cubic meters. Over the past eight decades, these infrastructure projects have helped avoid an estimated 10.09 trillion yuan (around 1.5 trillion U.S. dollars) in economic losses from floods, Wei said. Efforts to curb soil erosion have also produced substantial results. Zhu Xiaoyong, director of the commission's soil and water conservation bureau, presented data showing that 290,500 square km of land affected by soil erosion across the river basin have been rehabilitated. Soil and water conservation measures have kept about 24.7 billion tonnes of sediment from entering the river. The Yellow River spans multiple regions and forms an integrated ecosystem that requires coordinated cross-regional management. "After years of research, we have developed a reservoir operation approach that stores clean water while discharging sediment," said Zhang Jinliang, chief scientist of Yellow River Engineering Consulting Co., Ltd. "Precision water-sediment regulation marks a shift from passive response to proactive action in managing the river." Water allocation has also achieved better coordination. Since a unified water-management system covering all provincial-level regions along the river was introduced in 1999, the Yellow River has flowed uninterrupted for 27 consecutive years. Over the years, more efficient water use has helped expand irrigated farmland in the river basin to 132 million mu (8.8 million hectares). The basin and downstream irrigation areas produce roughly 89.5 billion kilograms of grain annually, or 13.3 percent of China's national grain output. YRCC figures also show that water quality in the Yellow River Basin has markedly improved. The proportion of monitoring sections graded Class I to III, indicating good water quality, rose from 59.1 percent in 2016 to 93.2 percent in 2025. The changes are also visible in communities along the river. Lyu's photographs documenting the Hukou Waterfall's shifting waterscape have helped boost local tourism. His widely shared photos have helped turn tourism into a pillar industry in a county that was once impoverished. "The Yellow River ecosystem forms an integrated whole," he said. "From headwater conservation in the upper reaches and soil and water conservation in the middle reaches to wetland restoration in the lower reaches, green has become a defining feature of high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin."

item.title: China's resident-led renewal efforts give old neighborhoods new life
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 08:19:00
This photo taken on Aug. 11, 2025 shows a view of the renewed neighborhood Zhegong Xincun in Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province. (Xinhua) Amid the ongoing urban renewal drive in China, residents in an east China neighborhood have spearheaded a new model by raising funds for rebuilding their dilapidated residential block. Unlike the government-led model that typically offers residents new apartments and cash compensation, this project saw its 548 homeowner households raise 499 million yuan (about 74.32 million U.S. dollars), more than 80 percent of the reconstruction bill, with the government covering the rest. The compound with 13 previously run-down buildings, known as Zhegong Xincun, sits in the downtown Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of the affluent Zhejiang Province. These six-story walk-ups were transformed into seven mid-rise buildings, surrounded by green spaces and shared facilities, in February last year. Hangzhou was an early adopter of this approach. It is among initiatives piloted across Chinese cities, from Harbin in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province to Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province, to avoid large-scale land acquisition and heavy investment from developers. Such pilot projects address long-standing hurdles for urban regeneration in China. Small scattered plots often deliver slim returns for commercial developers, and matching residents' compensation expectations has frequently stalled renewal plans, said Wu Songtao, professor at the School of Architecture and Design of Harbin Institute of Technology. According to a State Council executive meeting held in May, China is shifting from the stage of large-scale incremental expansion to a stage focused on improving the quality and efficiency of existing urban stock. "Instead of large-scale demolition, the goal now is to revitalize existing buildings, factories, neighborhoods and public spaces," said Zheng Degao, vice president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design. Zheng added that all beneficiaries, namely government, businesses and property owners alike, should share both the costs and the benefits. But translating this vision into practice was no easy task. Renewing old neighborhoods involves many interests and is prone to disputes, said Li Yin, an official with Gongshu District. Previous attempts to renew Zhegong Xincun all failed due to residents seeing only limited benefits and strains on public finances. Built in the 1980s and 1990s as faculty housing for Zhejiang University of Technology, the compound sits in a prime location in central Hangzhou, surrounded by shopping areas, metro stations and a large hospital. However, over the years, safety hazards mounted. Stiff windows were difficult to close, and building settlement warped door frames and locks, sometimes forcing residents to climb over walls to enter their homes. "The plaster crumbled at the slightest touch. We lived in fear every day," said a resident surnamed Yu. The university once carried out reinforcement work, but the effect was limited. Because the buildings continued to tilt and crack due to ongoing building settlement, such measures offered only temporary relief. A previous housing-relocation plan failed to win broad support. According to residents, a 2014 survey on demolition and reconstruction, and another attempt in 2018, both came to nothing. "The old idea was that the government should cover everything, from relocation to renovation," one resident said. "But as previous plans kept falling through, we realized we had to do it ourselves." This photo taken on Aug. 11, 2025 shows a view of the renewed neighborhood Zhegong Xincun in Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province. (Xinhua) The turning point came in April 2023, when the subdistrict community office reached out to residents for their opinions on starting a resident-led renewal project. With support from local policies on renovating old urban neighborhoods, Gongshu District developed and adopted a resident-led renewal model for the compound. The initial stage of the renewal project was launched in mid-2022. The district set up a special task force to coordinate departments, study relevant policies and win public support via explanations. Local officials said that the harder part was reaching a consensus. "The core of the entire project lies in community engagement, shifting residents' mindset from being asked to renovate to wanting to renovate," Li said. A voluntary committee of 13 representatives was formed. After consulting all households, it submitted an application and entrusted local authorities to coordinate and initiate the renewal. By late August 2023, all but one of the compound's 548 homeowner households had signed agreements, bringing the signing rate to 99.82 percent, thus paving the way for the renewal plan to move forward. In May 2024, the last household came forward to sign before delivery. "This last resident later told me, 'I watched for a long time, and I could see the project is fair,'" Li said. Yu calculated that her original 76-square-meter apartment, plus an additional 19 square meters and a parking space, brought her total payment to nearly 980,000 yuan. "I originally bought the apartment for 1.51 million yuan. Even with this expense, my total cost remains below the market price, and I have more living space. I am also a beneficiary," she said. The project, though, has benefited from the community's demographics. Experts noted that although Zhegong Xincun is an aging community, its residents, mostly Zhejiang University of Technology faculty members and their families, are relatively better off, a factor that helped the project move forward. When the project was launched, the community also had a large elderly population, with 208 residents aged 80 or above and 36 aged 90 or above. Some feared a long construction period might keep them from returning, while others with children overseas faced the daunting task of relocating alone. To address these concerns, the working group provided comprehensive support. Ambulances were arranged to escort several residents over 90 on the moving day. Transitional housing was secured and rented to elderly residents, refurbished with age-friendly features such as shower seats and toilet grab bars. The compound was handed over last year, with about 70 percent of households having moved in, and they have begun renovating their new homes. The approach of Zhegong Xincun aligns with China's grand roadmap to advance urban renewal as the country endeavors to create safer, greener and more comfortable cities, while fostering new growth momentum. Under the urban renewal plan during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to renovate 500,000 units of dilapidated urban housing and 115,000 old urban residential communities. It supports resident-led renewal and on-site demolition and reconstruction of old housing, while exploring sustainable operation models. "This resident-led renewal model has opened a new path for urban renewal in China," said Xu Lin, a professor at Zhejiang University, noting that as China's urbanization enters a new phase, cities are no longer expanding through large-scale demolition and construction, but focusing on improving living conditions for residents. "At the end of the day, it's about giving people a better life," said Xu.

item.title: A five-euro 'toll': Europe shouldn't be penny-wise and pound-foolish: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 00:23:00
Photo taken on September 3, 2026 shows e-commerce parcels stored at a warehouse near Liege Airport in Grace-Hollogne, Belgium. Photo: VCG The five-euro charge needs to be viewed in the context of the overall scale of China-EU trade. The nature of this policy is even more worthy of deep consideration. Such a penny-wise, pound-foolish approach may appear to bolster government coffers in the short term, but it comes at the expense of Europe's long-term economic vitality. It will also create unnecessary friction in the mutually beneficial economic and trade relationship between China and the EU, ultimately harming Europe's own development interests. The European Union (EU) has imposed a so-called two-euro "handling fee" on packages from outside the bloc to European consumers since Sunday. Combined with the three-euro charge introduced in July on small packages worth less than 150 euros, this new revenue-grabbing levy brings the fixed customs-clearance costs on a low-value parcel to five euros. What's more, the handling fee will be levied separately for each category of goods in the same parcel. For example, if a parcel contains three categories of goods, the handling fee will amount to six euros, regardless of how many items fall into each category. Given that approximately 93 percent of cheap packages that entered the EU came from China, the move is widely seen as being clearly targeted at Chinese goods. The five-euro charge needs to be viewed in the context of the overall scale of China-EU trade. More importantly, the nature of this policy is even more worthy of deep consideration. The figures tell a revealing story: 5.9 billion parcels annually, a fixed charge of three to five euros per package, and an annual revenue boost of six billion euros for the EU budget. Combined with the rule allowing fees to accumulate across different product categories, this measure has gone well beyond the traditional role of tariffs in regulating trade. It effectively amounts to an "entry tax" imposed on consumers even before they complete their purchases. Europe once built its identity on free trade. Yet it is now turning into an economy that charges tolls at its own doorstep, parcel by parcel. The more lucrative this toll-collecting business becomes, the further Europe drifts from its original principles. The money may flow into EU coffers, but ordinary European consumers will bear the costs. The EU claims that the new fee will be paid by platforms and sellers. However, e-commerce platform AliExpress has explicitly warned that the charges would hurt low-income households in Europe and "exacerbate the cost-of-living crisis." The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) has also expressed concern that some platforms may try to pass these new costs onto consumers at the final stages of the purchase. A three-euro trinket subject to an additional five euros in charges would end up costing more in taxes than the product itself. It is clear whom this kind of measure is really "protecting." A new wave of protests is currently spreading across Europe. Although the specific demands vary, protesters share common concerns over inadequate public investment and the rising cost of living. The EU's decision to introduce a "toll" on small parcels is, in essence, an attempt to shift its fiscal anxieties onto ordinary citizens through administrative measures. Imposing additional charges on low-value parcels amid high inflation will hit European consumers even harder, and will exacerbate mounting tensions over people's livelihoods and further inflame already strained public sentiment. At a deeper level, such a short-sighted policy choice exposes Europe's strategic confusion amid profound changes in the global economic and trade landscape. Faced with the rapid growth of cross-border e-commerce and the competitive advantages brought about by China's industrial upgrading, Europe has chosen not to address these challenges by strengthening its own industrial competitiveness and improving the efficiency of its internal market. Instead, it has reverted to the old path of trade protectionism, using administrative barriers to fragment global supply chains. This approach not only runs counter to the free trade principles Europe has long championed but also undermines its credibility in shaping global economic and trade rules. Such a penny-wise, pound-foolish approach may appear to bolster government coffers in the short term, but it comes at the expense of Europe's long-term economic vitality. It will also create unnecessary friction in the mutually beneficial economic and trade relationship between China and the EU, ultimately harming Europe's own development interests. Tariff barriers cannot resolve Europe's structural problems. The price advantages of Chinese e-commerce stem from the efficiency of its industrial and supply chains, rather than merely from a tax exemption policy. The EU may be able to keep goods out of its market, but it cannot make its domestic supply chains equally efficient overnight. Some European business representatives have put the calculation more bluntly: US tariff hikes have already pushed up the price of European wines in North America by 15 to 25 percent compared with three years ago. Now, with procurement costs from China rising as well, some European buyers are turning to US platforms instead. "Who is the ultimate winner? American companies." In stark contrast to this wall-building approach lies another path to development. China-EU trade and investment consultations have yielded multiple results, BYD's factory in Hungary is set to begin mass production, the China-Switzerland free trade agreement has been upgraded, and China's hybrid car exports to the EU surged by more than 200 percent year on year in September. On the same continent, two different choices are producing two different outcomes: those building walls are reaping anxiety, while those embracing openness are securing orders. The small-parcel levy is just one of several restrictive measures introduced by the EU this year. Europe was once among the champions of free trade, yet it is now "closing" its doors through measures that amount to squeezing every last penny out of consumers. Genuine competitiveness is forged through market competition. Translating anxiety into tax rates will only cause Europe to fall further behind amid the technological revolution, while forcing ordinary households to foot the bill for political maneuvering. China and the EU are important economic and trade partners. And China maintains that an open and inclusive international trading environment serves the common interests of all parties. Whether Europe chooses to narrow that door further or open it again is a question whose answer is already clear.

item.title: GT Voice: What will open the door to $1t export club for S.Korea, others?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 23:02:00
A view of SK hynix's headquarters building in Icheon, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, on October 28, 2026. Photo: VCG The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is propelling South Korea toward a $1 trillion export milestone. Its exports totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of the year, putting the country on track to become the fourth nation, after the US, China and Germany, to surpass $1 trillion in annual exports, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Monday. What lies behind South Korea's bid to join the $1 trillion export club? Several factors are at play, but one deserves particular attention: the global AI boom. International discussions of AI sometimes focus on the contest for technological leadership. Yet the economic demand stemming from the rapid development of AI deserves far greater attention. This demand is helping South Korea knock on the door of the $1 trillion export club. The force of AI demand is clearly visible in South Korea's October export figures. Semiconductor exports jumped 259.4 percent to $56.44 billion, reflecting continued heavy investment by global technology companies in the AI industry. Computer exports soared 496.6 percent to $5.85 billion, as the spread of AI services drove greater investment in server infrastructure. Electrical equipment exports increased 74 percent to $1.99 billion, reflecting rising demand for transformers, wires, cables, and other equipment used in AI data centers. These figures point to a much bigger story. The global expansion of AI is generating enormous demand across industries. This is a powerful new source of growth for manufacturers and exporters around the world. The 2025 World Trade Report issued by the World Trade Organization (WTO) estimates that with the right enabling policies, AI could boost the value of cross-border flows of goods and services by nearly 40 percent by 2040, thanks to productivity gains and lower trade costs. South Korea's export figures raise two broader questions. First, can the country cross the $1 trillion threshold and sustain that level of exports? Second, could more economies join the club in the years ahead? The WTO's projections offer grounds for considering both possibilities. If AI continues to fuel global trade growth, the $1 trillion export club may have more members in the years ahead. To tap into this demand, it is first necessary to understand what drives it. AI is not a single product or industry, but a complex, layered system built on semiconductors, data, computing infrastructure, energy, models and applications. South Korea's export figures offer a glimpse of just how finely specialized this supply chain has become. Alongside chips and computers, exports include transformers, wires, cables and other equipment needed to power and operate AI data centers. These components and capabilities are closely interconnected, linking companies and economies in a global network of production and trade. Within this global network, China is becoming an increasingly important market as its AI industry advances rapidly. South Korea's trade figures offer a telling example. In October, its exports to China rose 133.6 percent to $26.98 billion, with semiconductors and wireless communication devices among the major export items. China's expanding technology sector is generating demand that reaches beyond its borders. That picture is difficult to reconcile with claims that China's demand is faltering. In September, China's imports grew at a double-digit rate, while exports also continued to expand. As China's technology exports grow, it continues to import goods, creating opportunities for suppliers in other economies. This two-way trade makes China an important participant in the expansion of global trade in the AI era. For South Korea to sustain its export growth, deeper integration into global supply chains and open trade will matter. The same applies to other economies seeking to join the $1 trillion export club. The WTO's World Trade Report emphasizes the importance of an open and predictable trading environment in ensuring that the benefits of AI are widely shared. For South Korea and other economies looking to expand their exports, deeper integration into global supply chains, stronger industrial cooperation and support for open trade may be the keys to unlocking the door to the $1 trillion export club.

item.title: When Nazi symbol becomes a Halloween prop in Japan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 22:39:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Halloween is a time for dressing up, but not every symbol makes for a fun costume. This year's Halloween in Japan brought the issue into focus. On Saturday evening, a post on the X platform drew widespread attention. The photos showed multiple Japanese participants displaying the Nazi swastika. The account was later temporarily suspended for violations of the platform's rules on hateful content. But the photos continued to circulate, drawing criticism from users around the world. Some comments were blunt: "So this is what peace loving nation Japan looks like." Others pointed out: "Japan NEVER paid for its war crimes," "A lot of Japanese ppl dont learn modern history from schools. It is very hard to make them understand why what they are doing over there is wrong." The situation points to a question: Why do such symbols seem to have lost much of their historical weight for some young Japanese people? As early as 2014, The Guardian ran a report on two key politicians of then Japanese cabinet who had been photographed smiling with Kazunari Yamada, the leader of a Japanese neo-Nazi group. Sanae Takaichi, then internal affairs minister, was one of them. Although she later tried to distance herself from Yamada, the fact that such a photo could be taken at all, had already exposed how loosely the lines were drawn between Japan's right-wing political establishment and neo-Nazi circles. The deeper problem lies in the state-led shaping of historical memory. The Japanese government has continued to revise history textbooks. This is no longer simply a matter of downplaying the past. It amounts to a systematic effort to erase the memory of wartime atrocities. In the latest high school textbooks, terms such as "comfort women" and "forced labor" have been replaced with expressions such as "recruited" and "mobilized." Descriptions of "aggression" are nowhere to be found, and relevant chapter titles have been changed to the so-called "The Manchurian Incident and the Rise of the Military." The history books children grow up reading are themselves designed to sidestep the central question: What did Japan actually do? Outside the classroom, popular culture does something else: It turns historical symbols into entertainment. Anime, video games, films and television dramas pull symbols out of their bloody historical context and turn them into material that can be collected, worn and consumed. Once a symbol is reduced to a "cool-looking design" on a piece of clothing, its moral weight is stripped away. In 2016, the Japanese idol group Keyakizaka46 faced international backlash after wearing outfits resembling Nazi uniforms. During the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, Japanese fans were stopped by security personnel from displaying Rising Sun flags in the stands. These incidents point to the same question: Why does Japanese society repeatedly find itself embroiled in similar controversies whenever symbols linked to its wartime past appear? Germany offers a stark contrast. Under German law, publicly displaying symbols linked to Nazi organizations is a criminal offense. Violations can result in a fine or up to three years in prison. Japan has no comparable legal boundary. And worse, many people, including high-level politicians, continue to worship at notorious Yasukuni Shrine, which enshrines Class-A war criminals from WWII. Over time, the next generation has grown increasingly detached from the idea that the bloody history must be remembered. The real danger is not the mere appearance of these symbols, but the gradual loss among young Japanese people of any sense of the evil they represent. When Nazi symbols can be casually turned into Halloween props, what this reveals is not simply the ignorance of a few individuals, but a systemic distortion of historical understanding. In the minds of some young Japanese people, the gravity of aggression, genocide and responsibility for war has been hollowed out. The swastika displayed in Japan during Halloween is merely one visible fragment of a much larger problem. And it's a warning that when distortions of historical memory are repeatedly tolerated, they eventually become a systematic erosion of our shared understanding of the past. Japan has long sought to diminish the weight of its own wartime crimes. When it invaded and brutally ravaged Asia, it called its aggression "liberation." The world, especially Asia, has watched this script play out before. It must not pretend it does not recognize the script.
